title: Philosophy & Logic
summary: Deductive validity, formal fallacies, and sound reasoning evaluated by pure logical form.

objectives.title: Deductive validity depends only on formal argument structure
Soundness requires both deductive validity and true premises
Modus ponens and modus tollens are valid deductive forms
Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid forms

body.text: Deductive logic assesses arguments by their logical form, not whether their premises happen to be true in the real world.
An argument is deductively valid if and only if: whenever all premises are true, the conclusion must necessarily be true. A valid argument can have completely false premises.
An argument is sound only when it satisfies two requirements: (1) its logical form is valid, and (2) every premise is factually true.
Always distinguish validity (structural truth preservation) from soundness (valid structure with factual premises).

steps.title: Assessing deductive validity

body.text: Evaluate the logical form of this argument alone, setting aside whether the claims are factually true:

Premise 1: All moons are made of green cheese.
Premise 2: Phobos is a moon.
Conclusion: Therefore, Phobos is made of green cheese.
Is this argument deductively valid in its logical form?

options.text: Valid: if both premises were true, the conclusion would necessarily follow.
Invalid: the first premise is empirically false in the real world.

misconceptions.invalid: Validity concerns formal structure, not factual truth. Because the conclusion follows inevitably from the premises, the argument is structurally valid even with false premises.

hints: Ask what happens in a hypothetical world where both premises are true.
Does the conclusion follow from the structure of the premises, regardless of empirical facts?
An argument can be structurally valid while being factually unsound.

correct.text: Correct. Deductive validity is purely structural. If the premises were true, the conclusion would necessarily follow. (The argument is unsound because premise 1 is false, but its deductive form is valid.)

solution.text: Answer: Valid. Form: All M are C; P is M; therefore P is C.

steps.title: Evaluating validity and soundness

body.text: Read the argument and determine its deductive status:

Premise 1: All mammals have lungs.
Premise 2: Whales are mammals.
Conclusion: Therefore, whales have lungs.
Which classification applies to this argument?

options.text: Deductively valid and sound.
Deductively valid, but unsound.
Invalid in logical form.

misconceptions.valid-unsound: Soundness requires valid form plus true premises. Since both premises are biologically true and the form is valid, the argument is sound.
misconceptions.invalid: The structure preserves truth: if all M have L and W is M, W must have L. The form is valid.

hints: Check the logical form first: does the conclusion follow from the premises?
Check the premises second: are they factually true?
An argument that is both valid and has true premises is sound.

correct.text: Correct. The argument has valid logical form, and both premises are factually true, making it sound.

steps.title: Order of logical evaluation

body.text: Arrange the steps in the correct methodological order for evaluating whether an argument is sound.

items.text: 1. Analyze formal structure and test whether the argument is deductively valid.
2. Assess empirical evidence to verify whether all premises are factually true.
3. Conclude whether the argument meets the criteria for soundness.

hints: If an argument is invalid in form, checking premise truth cannot make it sound.
Form is evaluated first before investigating empirical premise truth.

correct.text: Correct. In formal analysis, test deductive validity first. If invalid, the argument is automatically unsound. If valid, verify premise truth next to determine soundness.

solution.text: 1. Check form (validity) -> 2. Check premises -> 3. Determine soundness.

body.text: A conditional statement `P -> Q` establishes that whenever antecedent P is true, consequent Q must be true.

Two foundational valid deductive rules:
- Modus Ponens: From `P -> Q` and `P`, conclude `Q`.
- Modus Tollens: From `P -> Q` and `~Q`, conclude `~P`.

Two common invalid formal fallacies:
- Affirming the Consequent: From `P -> Q` and `Q`, concluding `P` is INVALID.
- Denying the Antecedent: From `P -> Q` and `~P`, concluding `~Q` is INVALID.
Notice the symmetry: affirming the antecedent or denying the consequent is valid; affirming the consequent or denying the antecedent is a fallacy.

steps.title: Name the pattern (1)

body.text: Consider the formal structure below:

Premise 1: P -> Q
Premise 2: P
Conclusion: Q
Based purely on its logical form, what is this deductive pattern?

options.text: Modus Ponens (valid deductive form).
Affirming the Consequent (invalid fallacy).
Denying the Antecedent (invalid fallacy).

misconceptions.ac: Premise 2 affirms P (the antecedent), not Q (the consequent).

hints: Which part of the conditional `P -> Q` is affirmed in Premise 2?
Affirming the antecedent (P) leads validly to the consequent (Q).

correct.text: Correct. Modus Ponens affirms the antecedent P to validly deduce consequent Q.

solution.text: Answer: Modus Ponens (P -> Q, P |= Q).

steps.title: Valid or invalid? (form A)

body.text: Consider this formal argument structure:

Premise 1: P -> Q
Premise 2: Q
Conclusion: P
Based on logical form alone, is this argument valid or invalid?

options.text: Invalid: the premises could be true while the conclusion is false.
Valid: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true.

misconceptions.valid: Modus Ponens requires knowing P, not Q. Knowing Q does not guarantee that P occurred; Q could be true for an entirely different reason.

hints: Can Q be true even if P is false?
Look for a truth assignment where both premises are true but the conclusion is false.
If P is false and Q is true, `P -> Q` is true, Q is true, but P is false. This counterexample proves invalidity.

correct.text: Correct. This is the fallacy of Affirming the Consequent. The truth assignment { P: false, Q: true } satisfies both premises while falsifying the conclusion, proving the form is invalid.

steps.title: Name the pattern (2)

body.text: Consider the formal structure below:

Premise 1: P -> Q
Premise 2: ~Q
Conclusion: ~P
Based purely on its logical form, what is this deductive pattern?

options.text: Modus Tollens (valid).
Denying the Antecedent (invalid fallacy).
Affirming the Consequent (invalid fallacy).

misconceptions.da: Premise 2 denies Q (the consequent), not P (the antecedent).
misconceptions.ac: Premise 2 is a negation, not an affirmation.

hints: Premise 2 denies the consequent Q.
If P would require Q, and Q is false, what must P be?

correct.text: Correct. Modus Tollens denies the consequent (~Q) to validly infer the negation of the antecedent (~P).

steps.title: Valid or invalid? (form B)

body.text: Consider this formal argument structure:

Premise 1: P -> Q
Premise 2: ~P
Conclusion: ~Q
Based on logical form alone, is this argument valid or invalid?

options.text: Invalid: the premises could be true while the conclusion is false.
Valid: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true.

misconceptions.valid: Modus Tollens requires denying the consequent (~Q). Denying the antecedent (~P) is a formal fallacy.

hints: If P is false, does that force Q to be false?
Test assignment { P: false, Q: true }. Is `P -> Q` true? Is `~P` true? Is `~Q` true?

correct.text: Correct. This is the fallacy of Denying the Antecedent. When P is false and Q is true, both premises are true but conclusion ~Q is false.

steps.title: Complete the derivation

body.text: Complete the conclusion so that the inference rule is a valid Modus Tollens deduction:

hints: Modus Tollens concludes the negation of the antecedent.
Write the negation of variable P.

correct.text: Correct. From `P -> Q` and `~Q`, the valid conclusion is `~P`.

reviews.title: Review: chained conditionals

body.text: Evaluate the formal validity of this argument structure:

Premise 1: P -> Q
Premise 2: Q -> R
Conclusion: P -> R
Judging by logical form alone, is this argument valid or invalid?

options.text: Valid: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true.
Invalid: the premises could be true while the conclusion is false.

misconceptions.invalid: Hypothetical Syllogism is deductively valid. If P implies Q and Q implies R, P must imply R.

hints: If P is true, what does Premise 1 say about Q?
If Q is true, what does Premise 2 say about R?

correct.text: Correct. Hypothetical Syllogism (P -> Q, Q -> R |= P -> R) is deductively valid in formal logic.

reviews.title: Review: valid form with a false premise

body.text: An argument has flawless, deductively valid logical form. However, one of its premises is factually false. What is the status of this argument?

options.text: Deductively valid, but unsound.
Invalid in form.
Sound, because form takes precedence.

misconceptions.invalid: A false premise does not invalidate the argument's formal structure.
misconceptions.sound: An argument cannot be sound if any premise is false.

hints: Validity is property of the form; soundness requires truth of the premises.

correct.text: Correct. The argument retains its valid logical form, but fails the requirement for soundness because of the false premise.

reviews.title: Review: valid or invalid?

body.text: Evaluate the formal structure:

Premise 1: R -> S
Premise 2: ~S
Conclusion: ~R
Based on logical form alone, is this argument valid or invalid?

options.text: Valid: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true.
Invalid: the premises could be true while the conclusion is false.

misconceptions.invalid: Modus Tollens is valid: denying the consequent guarantees the negation of the antecedent.

hints: If R implies S, and S did not occur, could R have occurred?

correct.text: Correct. Modus Tollens (R -> S, ~S |= ~R) is valid.

reviews.title: Review: valid or invalid?

body.text: Evaluate the formal structure:

Premise 1: R -> S
Premise 2: ~R
Conclusion: ~S
Based on logical form alone, is this argument valid or invalid?

options.text: Invalid: the premises could be true while the conclusion is false.
Valid: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true.

misconceptions.valid: This denies the antecedent (~R), not the consequent (~S). It is an invalid formal fallacy.

hints: Does ~R guarantee ~S, or could S still occur through other causes?
Assignment R=false, S=true makes premises true and conclusion false.

correct.text: Correct. Denying the Antecedent is invalid. Counterexample: R=false, S=true.
